description: We are passionate about space exploration, technology, and creating engaging educational experiences. Our team combines software development, 3D visualization, game design, and NASA data to build interactive space-mission experiences.
summary:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive 3D browser game that lets students experience the responsibilities of a lunar astronaut and mission commander. Players fly from Earth to the Moon, manage a five-person crew, build and operate a lunar outpost, balance power, food, water, oxygen, and materials, respond to solar particle storms, explore the lunar surface with a rover, and eventually prepare the crew for the journey home.

The game turns real space science and NASA data into hands-on mission decisions. Players must understand resource tradeoffs, protect the crew during hazardous conditions, and plan sustainable operations rather than simply follow a predetermined story. NASA and NOAA reference data are presented alongside clearly labeled simulated mission readings, helping players distinguish real scientific information from gameplay systems.

The goal is to make lunar exploration more understandable, engaging, and educational by allowing students to learn through decisions, consequences, exploration, and mission survival.
details:
What the project does

Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a browser-based 3D mission simulation designed around the experience of operating a lunar mission from launch through return to Earth.

The experience begins with an Earth-to-Moon flight. Players complete launch and spacecraft preparation procedures, configure navigation, manage onboard systems, respond to incidents, perform the lunar braking and landing sequence, and reach the lunar surface.

After landing, players operate a timed lunar outpost. They manage power, food, water, oxygen, and construction materials while assigning a five-person crew to different jobs. The crew consists of specialists in power engineering, life support, botany, crew safety, and communications.

Players construct facilities such as solar arrays, battery banks, and greenhouses. Each facility introduces tradeoffs. For example, the greenhouse can produce food but requires power and water. Players therefore have to balance immediate survival requirements with long-term sustainability.

The outpost also introduces solar particle storm events. Players receive warnings, recall crew members to shelter, manage exposure risk, and deal with incidents affecting systems such as solar power and recycling. Running out of critical resources or exposing the crew during a storm can interrupt or end the mission.

The game also includes a lunar rover. Players can drive across the lunar terrain, search for supply caches, recover cargo, and return resources to the outpost. An educational historical exhibit connects exploration activities with Apollo missions and lunar geology.

Eventually, players can prepare a departure window and play through lunar liftoff, Earth transfer, reentry, parachute deployment, and splashdown. A final debrief reports mission performance and provides a score based on survival, resource management, sustainable operations, and exploration.

How it works

The game uses a combination of mission rules, resource simulation, crew assignment, timed events, browser saves, procedural 3D scenes, and interactive interfaces.

The lunar outpost operates on an accelerated mission clock. Players can pause the mission and change the simulation speed. Resource rates are shown directly in the HUD so players can understand how decisions affect the mission.

Crew members travel to assigned facilities and perform jobs over time. Construction also takes time and consumes materials. Storm events temporarily change the operational constraints of the outpost, requiring the player to make decisions about crew safety and resource continuity.

The game separates simulated mission variables from external scientific information. NASA and NOAA readings are displayed with source and timestamp information, while simulated values are visibly identified as gameplay data.

Educational and practical benefits

The project teaches systems thinking through gameplay. Instead of presenting space science only as information to memorize, it gives players interconnected problems to solve.

Players learn that:

  • power affects other life-support and production systems;
  • food, water, and oxygen are finite resources;
  • infrastructure requires time and materials;
  • crew assignments affect mission productivity;
  • hazardous space-weather conditions can change operational decisions;
  • exploration requires balancing scientific goals with crew safety;
  • successful missions require planning for both the present situation and the return journey.

The game therefore combines STEM education, resource management, space exploration, and interactive storytelling.

NASA and scientific data

The project uses NASA data and references throughout the experience. It includes NASA OSDR ISS cabin CO₂ measurements and an Artemis II trajectory dataset. The game also references NASA's DONKI archive for the solar-particle training scenario and NASA Apollo mission material for the historical lunar exhibit.

NASA and NOAA values can also be requested from the communications/control systems during gameplay. External readings are displayed separately from simulated mission values, with source and UTC timestamp information.

The game clearly distinguishes archival/reference data from simulated gameplay data.

Technology

The project is implemented as a TypeScript browser application using Vite and Three.js.

Major technologies include:

  • TypeScript
  • Three.js
  • Vite
  • HTML/CSS
  • Browser storage for mission saves
  • Web Audio API for mission audio
  • Netlify functions for optional external telemetry aggregation
  • NASA and NOAA public data sources

The spacecraft, lunar terrain, outpost, astronauts, rover, facilities, and other gameplay visuals are rendered using Three.js and procedural scene elements. The project also includes a static outpost fallback for environments without WebGL.

The application can be built into a static web deployment and is configured for deployment through Netlify.

Creativity

The central creative approach is to transform lunar mission planning into an interactive game rather than a conventional educational presentation.

The player is responsible for the consequences of decisions. Building infrastructure, allocating astronauts, managing resources, responding to space-weather hazards, exploring with a rover, and deciding when to return all form one connected mission.

This creates a progression from astronaut training to lunar operations and finally to crew recovery, giving the player a complete mission narrative rather than an isolated mini-game.

Intended impact

The project aims to help students develop curiosity about space science and understand the complexity of human lunar exploration.

By allowing players to experiment with resources, hazards, crew assignments, and exploration objectives, the project makes concepts such as life support, space weather, sustainability, engineering tradeoffs, and mission planning tangible and memorable.
